one_liner: Header-only C++17 counter-based RNGs (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche) for CPU and CUDA/HIP; beats stateful cuRAND in a Brownian dynamics run and std::mt19937 on short streams.
what_it_does: OpenRAND gives each work unit (particle, pixel) its own reproducible stream: you construct a generator on the spot from a 64-bit seed (32-bit for Squares) and a 32-bit counter, draw a few numbers, and throw it away, so no per-thread state lives in global memory and results do not depend on thread count. Generators expose rand<T>() for 32/64-bit ints and [0,1) floats, uniform(low, high), range(N), randn() (Box-Muller), gamma(), plus Philox's draw_int4/draw_float4, and they satisfy the C++ UniformRandomBitGenerator interface so std:: distributions work on them. It is not a drop-in std::mt19937 replacement: the seeding model is (seed, counter) per work unit rather than one long-lived engine.
how_it_is_fast: Counter-based generation: each output is a keyed bijection of (seed, counter) computed in registers (Philox-4x32-10 multiply/xor rounds, Threefry-2x32-20 add-rotate-xor, Widynski's Squares middle-square rounds, or the Tyche ARX mix), so construction is a few register moves instead of mt19937's 624-word seeding or a cuRAND state load/store. On the GPU the win in the paper comes from skipping curand_init and the per-thread state round trip to global memory (about 64 MB saved per million particles), not from a faster Philox; on the CPU it comes from cheap construction for short streams.
when_to_use: CUDA or HIP kernels where each thread or particle needs a few random numbers per launch and you want to stop storing curandState arrays; the paper measured 1.8x over cuRAND Philox on an A100 and 1.7x on a V100 in a RNG-bound Brownian dynamics kernel.
Simulations that must be bitwise reproducible regardless of thread count or scheduling (seed = particle id, counter = timestep).
CPU code that constructs many short-lived generators (10 to 1,000 draws each), where std::mt19937's seeding cost dominates.
Code that must compile unchanged for host, CUDA and HIP from one header set with no intrinsics or platform-specific code.
when_not_to_use: Long single streams on the CPU: at 10K draws only Tyche and Squares beat std::mt19937 (roughly 3.5-4x); Philox is slightly slower and Threefry about 6x slower, and SIMD or small-state generators (xoshiro, PCG, Romu) are faster still.
Already on Random123: the paper shows OpenRAND Philox on par with Random123 (1.78 s versus 1.81 s on A100), so the gain is API simplicity, not speed.
More than 2^32 draws from one (seed, counter) pair: the paper states each stream has period 2^32 and the internal counter is a uint32_t.
You need the published Squares64 output: open issue #25 reports the 64-bit Squares path differs from Widynski's paper.
Cryptographic use: these are reduced-round statistical generators, not CSPRNGs.

integration.form: header-only (include/openrand/*.h; CMake INTERFACE target OpenRAND::OpenRAND, FetchContent or make install)
integration.dependencies: none (Google Test, Google Benchmark, TestU01 and PractRand only for optional tests/benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (if constexpr, std::void_t); CMake 3.18 if using the CMake target; nvcc for CUDA, hipcc for HIP
integration.platforms: any C++17 host; NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA (__host__ __device__ through the OPENRAND_DEVICE macro) and AMD GPUs via HIP; no architecture-specific intrinsics
integration.thread_safety: Generators are small value types with no shared or global state; the intended pattern is one generator per thread/work unit, so no synchronization is needed. Sharing one instance across threads is unsynchronized (not documented).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: satisfies the UniformRandomBitGenerator interface (32-bit result_type) so it can replace std::mt19937 inside std:: distributions, but the constructor takes (seed, counter) and the stream model differs; against cuRAND it replaces curand_init/curand_uniform with a different API

gotchas: Philox::draw<uint32_t>() (used by operator() and rand<float>()) computes a full 4x32 Philox block and returns only one word, discarding three; use draw_int4()/draw_float4() to get all four, which is why scalar Philox loses to mt19937 on long CPU streams.

rand<float>() and rand<double>() are documented as [0,1) but the u01 conversion (x * 2^-32 + 2^-33 in float) rounds to exactly 1.0f for the top 128 uint32 inputs (about 1 in 33.5 million draws), and to 1.0 for the top 1,024 uint64 inputs in double (derived from the base_state.h code, not documented upstream); clamp before using the value as an index.
range<T>(N) defaults to the biased multiply-shift (biased=true); pass range<false>(N) for unbiased Lemire rejection. randn() discards the second Box-Muller value; use randn2().

squares.h does #define K 0xc58efd154ce32f6d at global scope, which breaks any including code that uses K as an identifier; Philox, Threefry and Squares have const members, so they are copy-constructible but not copy-assignable.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick OpenRAND for portable GPU and CPU code that wants stateless per-work-unit streams with a two-line API; vphilox and benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD are faster for bulk Philox output on CPUs with AVX, and the standalone Squares generator or Random123 give the same algorithms with lower-level APIs. For CPU throughput or attack resistance, Randen, Randompack or a SIMD xoshiro fit better.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' SoftwareX paper timed a 2D Brownian dynamics simulation (1M particles, 10,000 steps, Philox in every library, whole-process wall time, nvcc -O3 -std=c++17 -arch=sm_80) at 1.78 s with OpenRAND versus 3.20 s with cuRAND and 1.81 s with Random123 on an A100 SXM, and 2.48 s versus 4.23 s and 2.46 s on a Tesla V100 PCIe. Their CPU micro-benchmark on a Xeon Platinum 8260 against libstdc++ std::mt19937 (constructing a fresh engine per iteration; compiler and flags unstated) is only a log-scale chart: all four generators win on 10-100 draws, while at 10K draws only Tyche and Squares stay ahead.
status_note: Stale since 2024-12-11 (37 stars, CMake project version 1.0, release issue #9 still open) but MIT-licensed and small (the paper counts 470 source lines of core headers at publication), so it is easy to vendor.
